description: We are a Latinoamerican team formed by 3 Colombians and 1 Ecuadorian. Our team owns experience in web development, cross-platform applications, AI-driving development, software architecture, integration of LLMs and agentic workflows. The topic that we selected is related with the red planet, because we want to develop a solution that will help astronauts optimize their daily duties when they arrive to Mars by implementing a geolocation system, guiding them across the planet.
summary: Red Condors is a practice map built to plan one day on Mars for the NASA Space Apps challenge Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map. You can switch between a 3D globe and a flat map made with NASA Mars Trek images, mixing the Viking color map with MOLA height shading. Clicking on official IAU and USGS place names opens a card with photos, size details, and the story behind the name. Around Olympus Mons, seven pretend camps sit on real ground features and are clearly marked as fake. To plan a route, you just drop Start and End pins on a landmark or empty ground. Inside the Olympus laser-height area, the app finds the path that takes the least energy to travel. It adds up three things: the energy needed to climb against Mars gravity (3.71 m/s^2), the one-time energy needed to get up to cruising speed, and the steady effort needed to keep rolling. Every trip has strict slope limits to keep travellers safe.
details: A person walking stops if a hill is steeper than 15 degrees, a pretend crew car stops at 18 degrees, and a rover stops at 25 degrees. The map also tries to keep walks under eight hours. Outside this special height-checked zone, paths just draw a straight line without checking hills. If you use Street View in Jezero Crater, you can see real surface photos taken by the Perseverance rover. Red Condors is just a practice tool and not an official NASA product, but it shows how future explorers might plan their trips on Mars.
